body_markdown:
Porsche’s much-anticipated mid-engined two-seat Mission S concept car just broke cover at an event in New York. Like the Mission E before it, which previewed the production Taycan EV, this “super sports car” won’t remain a concept for long.


Porsche was careful with how it characterized the Mission E in its press release: “Above the iconic 911 sports car, Porsche is planning, for the first time, a permanently available super sports car offer.” Ahead of the event, senior executives confirmed to Hagerty that the Mission S will be built, and putting a mid-engined supercar into the segment above the 911 will put Porsche in direct competition with Ferrari.


The car’s looks were revealed early when it was caught being photographed on the same Queens pier as Porsche’s first mid-engined car, the 550 Spyder. But the leak won’t lessen the impact of Porsche announcing an entirely new sporting model that’s more powerful and expensive than the 911.


550 Spyder


Porsche


One word that does not feature prominently in the release? *Hypercar* . In fact, Dr. Michael Leiters, Chairman of the Executive Board of Porsche AG, characterizes it “not as a one-off hypercar,” which implies that there remains headroom in the Porsche lineup for a low-volume, even-higher-priced successor to the 918. Both the Mission S production car—no official name has been hinted at yet—and potential future hypercars fit Leiters’ plans to radically reshape Porsche, returning it to solid profits by cutting volumes and driving up pricing.


Details on what Porsche plans to put beneath the skin you see here are scant, and its leadership remains tight-lipped on the subject. The biggest open question is its powerplant; Porsche tuner RUF has an increasingly close relationship with the mothership, though it denies any plans to go in-house with Porsche, as AMG did with Mercedes and Alpina just recently did with BMW. However, RUF has developed a flat-eight engine, which was in the back of the[CTR3 prototype](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/ruf-enters-the-ring-with-a-heavyweight-boxer/) it showed at this year’s Goodwood Festival of Speed: That car’s rear engine cover remained notably sealed. We’re left wondering if that’s what’s hiding inside the Mission S.


Porsche


Indeed, the stacked quad pipes at the rear could hint at eight cylinders, but the rear venturi might be difficult to package below a low-mounted boxer engine. Both might easily change for production. Any of the 911’s top-end engine options could be transplanted into the Mission S to give it more than price-appropriate performance, but a new engine configuration along with the mid-engined layout would help differentiate the two. Hybrid power seems more likely for a long-lived, regular production model given ever-tightening emissions regulations, especially in Europe. There is a strong clamor from top-end supercar buyers for a return to natural aspiration and manual gearboxes, evidenced by the recently revealed[Gordon Murray S1](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/gordon-murray-special-vehicles-reveals-the-s1-a-v-12-powered-manual-equipped-stunner/) and[McLaren McL 6GT](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/the-mcl-6gt-does-something-mclaren-never-does-look-backwards/) , but Leiters might be saving those attractions for his low-volume specials.


The Mission S platform is understood to borrow heavily from the 911 and will be a hybrid of steel, aluminum, and carbon fiber rather than a bespoke carbon tub. Don’t get too excited by that fan mounted in the engine cover: it’s there for cooling, as it was on the 917 Le Mans car of the late ‘60s and early ‘70s, and not to suck the Mission S to the ground, as in the Gordon Murray T.50.


Porsche


This is the first car we’ve seen from Tobias Sühlmann, the new Head of Style at Porsche, and he hasn’t attempted to reinvent how Porsches look. Instead, the Mission S is a visual reflection of Leiters’ plan to refocus Porsche on what it does best, subtly referencing some of the marque’s greatest icons. (When the brand is in financial trouble, it tends to respond by playing the hits.) The “torpedo” fenders are pure Porsche; there’s a lot of late-‘90s GT1 in the flat nose and the “car-in-car” effect at the car’s tail, and some 959 in the rear section of the roofline. The wheels reference the lovely phone-dials of the 928. But while the details draw on disparate influences, Sühlmann has managed to pull it all together into a harmonious whole, the pinched waist lending the Mission S a more dramatic plan view than the 911, and greater inherent visual dynamism as a result.


Porsche


That back-to-basics theme continues inside, and Sühlmann’s cockpit design is likely to influence future Porsches beyond the production Mission S. Porsche describes it as “a deliberate return to the core values of sports car engineering” which “focuses on simplicity, clarity and intuitive operation;” all of which perhaps implies that its more recent cabin designs had drifted away from that.


Porsche


The basic cabin architecture is inspired by the 356 and 550, with two strong horizontal lines running from door to door across the dash. The most obvious visual change is the lack of a central screen: You replace it with your phone, held in place with a MagSafe connection, displaying navigation and able to control the car’s native functions via the My Porsche app. There’s a classic Porsche five-dial design to the digital dashboard, and you’ll be able to choose which era of 911 the dials recreate. But physical switches remain, including new push-pull organ-stop style controllers for the comfort and driving functions. There’s also now a key holder to the left of the steering wheel, as in Porsches of old, even if you no longer need it to turn an ignition barrel.


Porsche


The Mission S production car will be a central plank in Leiters’ “Sportwagenschmiede ‘35” strategy, which translates awkwardly to “sports car foundry.” It will undo some of what his predecessor (but also his current boss as CEO of the Volkswagen Group) Oliver Blume did when he also ran Porsche. Overall, volumes will be cut by around a third to 200,000 cars each year. Porsche has colossal brand power, so Leiters plans to capitalize on it by raising the average transaction price on its top 10,000 cars from €270,000 (about $303,000) to €330,000 (about $370,000). As the name suggests, there will be a greater focus on sports cars: not just the Mission S and another hypercar, but also a series of new and inventive ways for Porschephiles to spend money with the marque, including one-off and few-off specials under Porsche’s “sunderwunsch” (special wish) program, greater bespoke content on standard cars, and factory recommissioning of even relatively recent modern classics such as the Carrera GT.


Porsche


Porsche


Blume suggested late last year that the electric-specific platform of the forthcoming 718 could be re-engineered to take a combustion engine, but Leiters has nixed that notion for being too compromised. The slow-selling Taycan is likely to be folded into the Panamera range, but SUVs will remain an important profit source: The ICE Macan will return, and there will be a three-row SUV above the Cayenne, mainly for the U.S. market.


It’s a brave, far-reaching, and necessary reinvention of what Porsche makes and how it does business. Success is far from guaranteed, though, and the production Mission S will be both the emblem and the lightning rod for Michael Leiters’ tenure as CEO.
